0.title: Pastoral Care in Difficult Counseling Situations
0.overview:
This study is written for pastors, elders, and biblical counselors who find themselves sitting across from someone whose situation seems overwhelming -- an addiction that has destroyed a family, a mind that has broken under the weight of psychosis, a body ravaged by an eating disorder, a soul shattered by sexual violence. These are the hard cases. They do not yield quickly. They test the counselor's faith, patience, and theology.

Two convictions shape everything in this study. The first is the sufficiency of Scripture. The Word of God is 'living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit' (Heb. 4:12). It is 'profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work' (2 Tim. 3:16-17). This does not mean the biblical counselor is dismissive of medical science -- far from it. But it means that secular psychological frameworks are not granted equal authority alongside Scripture. The soul is addressed with the Word; the body is addressed with medicine. These are complementary, not competing.

The second conviction is the medical principle, emphasized by John Street, Stuart Scott, and the ACBC tradition: before drawing any spiritual or behavioural conclusions, always recommend a full medical examination. A thyroid condition can mimic depression. A neurological issue can produce strange thoughts. Alcohol withdrawal can be fatal without medical supervision. An eating disorder can reach a life-threatening weight. Rule out the physical first -- then address the heart.

Each unit follows the same structure: what is actually happening (biblically understood); see a doctor first; addressing the heart with Scripture; the means of grace and community; and, where life is at risk, the note on emergency referral. These are hard cases. But we serve a God who specialises in them.

1.title: Sexual Addiction: Pornography and the Captive Heart
1.overview:
Pornography addiction is one of the most common presenting problems in pastoral counseling today, and one of the least spoken about. The person who finally discloses it has typically carried the secret for years -- often decades -- and is drowning in shame. The pastoral failure mode is to respond with disgust or with moralistic pressure ('just stop') that the person has already applied to themselves thousands of times without success. Neither works. What is needed is a counselor who is neither shocked nor dismissive, who understands both the power of the addiction and the deeper heart issues driving it.

Biblically understood, pornography addiction is a form of sexual idolatry -- the pursuit of a counterfeit intimacy that promises what only God and covenant relationship can provide. Ed Welch's framework is helpful: addictions are 'a banquet in the grave' -- they offer a real but temporary pleasure that ultimately destroys. The heart behind the behavior must be addressed: What is the person seeking? Escape from pain? Intimacy they cannot find? Power and control? The answer will shape the counsel.

See a doctor first: Rule out testosterone imbalances or other hormonal issues. Also assess for depression or anxiety, which frequently co-occur and feed the addiction cycle.

Addressing the heart: The gospel of grace must be central -- shame drives the person deeper into secrecy and the addiction, not out of it. 'There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus' (Rom. 8:1) is not a licence for sin but the only ground on which genuine change becomes possible. Repentance, accountability, radical measures (Matt. 5:29), and the community of the church are the means of grace. Wives and families also need pastoral care -- the discovery of a spouse's addiction is a form of betrayal trauma.
1.theology: The theology of sexuality grounds the counsel. God created sexual desire as a good gift for the covenant of marriage (Gen. 2:24-25). The fall distorted this gift, turning it inward and toward counterfeit satisfactions. Pornography is not merely a bad habit; it is a form of worship -- giving to an image the devotion and desire that belongs to God and, within marriage, to a spouse. Jay Adams insisted that the biblical counselor must always ask 'what is the person doing instead of what God requires?' -- the answer reveals the idol. The path out is not willpower but worship reoriented: learning to find in Christ what the addiction falsely promises. Paul's instruction is clear: 'Flee sexual immorality' (1 Cor. 6:18) -- flee means run, not negotiate. And the positive counterpart: 'Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh' (Gal. 5:16).
1.examples: A married elder confesses to his pastor a 15-year pornography addiction. He has tried to stop hundreds of times. The pastor's first response is not a lecture but a question: 'When does it happen? What are you feeling right before?' The elder reveals it is always late at night, after conflict with his wife, when he feels rejected and alone. The addiction is medicating loneliness and marital pain. The counsel addresses both: the sexual sin directly, and the underlying marital disconnection and his pattern of emotional withdrawal. Accountability software, a confessional partner, and marital counseling running in parallel -- all grounded in the gospel of grace. Three years later the elder speaks at a men's retreat about freedom. He does not minimize what it cost. He does not minimize what grace did.

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's argument is theological, not merely moral: the body of the believer is the temple of the Holy Spirit. Sexual sin is not just a personal failure; it is a desecration of sacred space. 'You are not your own' -- the body belongs to God, purchased at the cost of the cross. This is not guilt-manipulation; it is identity. The person trapped in pornography has forgotten who they are and whose they are. Restoring that identity -- 'you are a temple; you are bought; you belong to God' -- is more powerful than any list of rules.

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus commands radical amputation -- not self-mutilation, but the ruthless removal of whatever provides access to sin. Applied to pornography: the internet filter is not optional, the smartphone in the bedroom is not negotiable, the late-night isolation must be broken. The person who says 'I want to change' but will not take radical practical measures has not yet understood the seriousness of what Jesus is saying. The radical measures are acts of faith -- concrete expressions of the desire to be free. The counselor helps the person identify their specific 'right eye' and remove it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel antidote to shame. The person addicted to pornography typically knows they are sinning; the knowledge has not produced change because it is buried under shame that drives them further into secrecy. 'No condemnation' does not minimise the sin -- it relocates the person. They are in Christ Jesus. Their identity is not 'pornography addict' but 'child of God who is struggling.' The counselor who communicates grace -- genuine, costly, unearned grace -- opens the door to honest disclosure, which is the first step to genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive command is as important as the negative prohibition. 'Flee' (1 Cor. 6:18) is only half the counsel; 'walk by the Spirit' is the other half. The person who merely stops the behavior without replacing it with Spirit-filled living will relapse -- the empty house will be reoccupied (Matt. 12:44-45). Accountability, Scripture meditation, prayer, corporate worship, genuine fellowship, marital intimacy -- these are the Spirit-filled alternatives that fill the space the addiction occupied. Change is not subtraction but substitution: replacing a false worship with the true one.

2.title: Eating Disorders: Identity, Control, and the Body
2.overview:
Anorexia and bulimia are among the most medically dangerous conditions a pastor will encounter. Anorexia has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition. This is not a phase, a diet gone wrong, or a vanity issue -- it is a life-threatening pattern of thought and behavior that must be taken with the utmost seriousness. The pastoral counselor who minimises it, spiritualises it prematurely, or works without medical involvement may contribute to a death.

See a doctor first -- urgently: This is non-negotiable. A person with suspected anorexia must be medically assessed immediately. Severe malnutrition impairs cognition, weakens the heart, and can cause sudden cardiac arrest. The counselor cannot do effective soul work with someone whose brain is starved of nutrition. Medical stabilisation comes first. In severe cases, inpatient treatment may be necessary. The pastor's role during this phase is presence, prayer, and support -- not primary counseling.

Biblically understood: Eating disorders are complex, but at their heart they typically involve a disordered search for identity, control, and worth. The person who restricts food is often saying: 'This is the one thing I can control in a world that feels out of control.' The person who purges is often managing overwhelming emotions they cannot otherwise process. The body has become the arena in which deep heart struggles -- fear, shame, worthlessness, perfectionism, the need for approval -- are being fought out.

Addressing the heart: Identity in Christ is the theological centre -- 'you are fearfully and wonderfully made' (Ps. 139:14) against the culture's and the person's own brutal self-assessment. The counselor must also explore the relational and family dynamics that typically underlie these disorders: perfectionist parents, histories of control, sometimes abuse. This is long, patient work.
2.theology: The Christian doctrine of the body is foundational. God created the body and called it good (Gen. 1:31). The incarnation affirms the body -- the Son of God took on flesh permanently. The resurrection guarantees the body's future -- we will be raised bodily (1 Cor. 15:44). The body is not a prison to be disciplined into submission; it is a temple to be cared for (1 Cor. 6:19-20). The eating disorder represents a profound theological distortion: the body is treated as the enemy, the site of shameful appetite, something to be controlled and punished. The gospel speaks directly into this distortion: the body is loved by God, redeemed by Christ, indwelt by the Spirit, and destined for resurrection glory. Stuart Scott's emphasis on renewing the mind (Rom. 12:2) is central here -- the deeply entrenched lies about the body and self-worth must be systematically replaced with the truth of Scripture.
2.examples: A 19-year-old university student is referred to her pastor by her concerned mother. She is visibly underweight. The pastor's first words are not about food or sin but about care: 'I am so glad you came. I want to understand what life feels like for you right now.' He listens for an hour. Then, gently but clearly: 'I am concerned about your physical health, and I want you to see a doctor this week -- not because I am passing you off, but because I want to be able to help your soul while someone is also caring for your body. Will you do that?' She agrees. The medical assessment reveals her heart is under strain. Inpatient stabilisation follows. The pastor visits. The biblical counseling begins in earnest six months later, when she is medically stable. The patience was not wasted -- it built the trust that made the deeper work possible.

verseByVerse.quote: For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Psalm is the theological counter-narrative to the eating disorder's core lie: 'My body is wrong, shameful, out of control, not enough.' God formed this body. He knitted it together with intentionality and care. It is 'fearfully and wonderfully made' -- the Hebrew conveys both awe and distinctiveness. The counselor who helps the person receive this verse -- not as a platitude but as a reality to be slowly believed -- is doing profound work. The journey from 'I hate my body' to 'I am fearfully and wonderfully made' is not quick, but it is the direction the gospel points.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The eating disorder is in large part a battle of the mind -- deeply entrenched beliefs about body, worth, control, and identity that have been reinforced over years. Paul's command is the prescription: 'be transformed by the renewal of your mind.' This is not a quick fix; it is a sustained process of replacing false beliefs with Scripture truth. The counselor identifies the specific lies ('I am only acceptable if I am thin,' 'I am disgusting,' 'controlling food is the only power I have') and works systematically through them with the Word. This is what makes biblical counseling distinct from secular therapy -- the authority and power of God's Word to actually renew the mind.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The body belongs to God -- it is his temple, purchased at the cost of his Son. To starve it, purge it, or wound it is not merely self-harm; it is the mistreatment of what belongs to God. This is not said to heap condemnation (the person with an eating disorder is already drowning in self-condemnation), but to reframe the issue theologically: 'You are not your own. This body is God's, and he loves it. Can we begin to care for what he has claimed?' The goal is stewardship born of love, not performance born of duty.

verseByVerse.quote: Because you are precious in my eyes, and honoured, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's direct address to his people -- 'you are precious in my eyes, and honoured, and I love you' -- strikes at the heart of the eating disorder's deepest lie: 'I am not enough; I am not worth loving as I am.' The person who has received this word from God -- really received it, not merely heard it -- finds the obsessive pursuit of a 'better' body beginning to loosen its grip. The counselor's task is to help the person hear this word as addressed to them, personally, bodily, as they actually are. God says 'precious' before any change has happened. That is the nature of grace.

3.title: Alcohol and Drug Addiction: Slavery, Freedom, and the Body
3.overview:
Alcohol and drug addiction combine physical dependency with profound heart issues -- which is precisely why both must be addressed and neither can be ignored. The pastor who addresses only the spiritual dimension while ignoring the physical is naive; the medical professional who addresses only the physical while ignoring the heart will see the person return again and again.

See a doctor first -- urgently: Alcohol withdrawal in a dependent person can be fatal -- it can cause seizures and death. Never tell an alcohol-dependent person to 'just stop drinking' without medical supervision. Drug withdrawal also carries serious physical risks depending on the substance. Medical detoxification under supervision is the necessary first step for physical dependency. The pastor's role during detox is prayer, presence, and preparation -- not primary counseling.

Biblically understood: Jay Adams was clear that the Bible addresses drunkenness as sin (Eph. 5:18; 1 Cor. 6:10) -- and the biblical counselor does not avoid this. But sin is not the whole picture: the person is also a sufferer, often medicating pain, trauma, loneliness, or despair that has never been addressed. Both dimensions must be held: the person is responsible for their choices AND they are suffering under a weight that has become crushing. Addressing only responsibility produces guilt without hope; addressing only suffering produces victimhood without change.

The heart questions: What does alcohol or the drug provide? Relief from anxiety? Escape from memories? A social identity ('I am a drinker')? The answer shapes the counsel. The community of the church -- not a substitute for medical care but essential alongside it -- is perhaps the most powerful force for sustained sobriety: real relationships, real accountability, real belonging.
3.theology: The biblical category of slavery is the most honest theological description of advanced addiction. 'Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin' (John 8:34). The person who began drinking by choice finds that choice increasingly narrowed until it feels like no choice at all -- the body craves, the mind rationalises, the will complies. Paul's description of the pre-conversion state is apt: 'slaves to various passions and pleasures' (Titus 3:3). The gospel announcement is liberation: 'You have been set free from sin and have become slaves of righteousness' (Rom. 6:18). This freedom is real but it is fought for -- 'work out your own salvation with fear and trembling' (Phil. 2:12) -- and it is sustained by the Spirit's power, not willpower alone. John Street's counsel is practical: the person must identify the triggers, flee the situations, build new habits, and be embedded in an accountable community.
3.examples: A 45-year-old man comes to his pastor after his wife has given him an ultimatum: sobriety or she leaves. He is drinking a bottle of whisky a day. The pastor's first action is to arrange a same-week appointment with his doctor -- explaining that stopping suddenly could be dangerous and that medical supervision is essential. The doctor manages a supervised withdrawal. Three weeks later, medically clear, the man begins biblical counseling. The pastor discovers a history of childhood abuse, decades of untreated shame, and a marriage full of unspoken pain. The alcohol was medicating all of it. The counseling addresses the shame with the gospel, the abuse with the truth of Psalm 34:18, and the marriage with Ephesians 5. Two years on, he is sober, his marriage is alive, and he leads a men's accountability group at the church. He is the most qualified person in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus names the condition with precision: slavery. The person who has tried to stop drinking and cannot is not merely weak-willed; they are experiencing the bondage that sin always produces when indulged over time. But the diagnosis is in the service of the promise: 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.' Not theoretically free, not free-with-an-asterisk, but free indeed. This freedom is the birthright of every believer -- and it is the goal of all addiction counseling. The counselor holds this promise out not as a slogan but as a reality to be pursued through repentance, community, and the Spirit's power.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's command gives both the prohibition and its positive alternative. 'Do not get drunk' -- the command is clear and non-negotiable, and the biblical counselor does not soften it. But 'be filled with the Spirit' is the deeper answer: the person who is genuinely, continuously filled with the Spirit finds in that filling what alcohol falsely promised -- comfort, courage, belonging, escape from anxiety. The addiction is a counterfeit of Spirit-filling. The counseling aims at the real thing: a life so filled with the Spirit that the counterfeit loses its appeal.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The person in addiction often believes they are uniquely weak, uniquely sinful, uniquely beyond hope. 'Common to man' -- your struggle is not unique. 'God is faithful' -- your sobriety does not rest on your faithfulness but on his. 'He will also provide the way of escape' -- for every specific temptation situation, God has prepared a specific exit. The counselor helps the person identify what those exits look like in practice: the phone call to make, the place to go, the prayer to pray, the verse to recite. Theology becomes strategy.

verseByVerse.quote: For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures... But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's past-tense description of his own pre-conversion state -- 'slaves to various passions and pleasures' -- is the counselor's own autobiography before it is the counselee's diagnosis. This produces humility: the counselor is not above the counselee but beside them, a fellow recipient of mercy. 'He saved us... according to his own mercy' -- not according to our track record, our resolve, or our performance. The person who has relapsed for the twentieth time needs to hear this: God's mercy is not exhausted by repeated failure. The door is still open. Come again.

4.title: Gambling: The Idol of Fortune and the Ruin It Brings
4.overview:
Gambling addiction is often overlooked in pastoral counseling literature, yet it is one of the most financially and relationally destructive patterns a pastor will encounter. The person in its grip has typically lost not only money but their family's savings, their home, their marriage, their self-respect -- and still cannot stop. The shame is enormous, the secrecy is almost universal, and the damage is often hidden until a crisis point.

See a doctor first: Pathological gambling is associated with high rates of depression and anxiety, which may have a physiological component. A medical assessment is important, as is a mental health screening. Suicidal ideation is significantly elevated among problem gamblers -- this must be assessed directly (see Unit 8).

Biblically understood: At its heart, gambling is an attempt to bypass the God-ordained means of provision -- work, faithfulness, stewardship -- and to find security and abundance through chance. It is a form of covetousness (the tenth commandment) combined with a failure to trust God's provision (Matt. 6:25-34). But more than that, for the compulsive gambler, the gambling itself has become an idol -- the thrill, the hope of the 'big win,' the temporary escape from reality. The idol promises what only God can give: transformation of circumstances, relief from anxiety, a sense of power and control over an uncertain future.

The practical damage must be addressed directly: debts must be disclosed, financial control must be handed over (often to a spouse or accountability partner), and access to gambling must be removed. This is not optional: the person who says they want to change but will not take these concrete steps is not yet ready to change. The family needs pastoral care as much as the gambler -- betrayal, financial ruin, and broken trust are the devastation left in the wake.
4.theology: The theology of contentment (Phil. 4:11; 1 Tim. 6:6-8; Heb. 13:5) is the positive framework for gambling addiction. The gambler has not learned contentment -- they are reaching, always reaching, for more, for the windfall that will finally make life feel secure and sufficient. The gospel reframes sufficiency: 'My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus' (Phil. 4:19). Not every want, but every need -- and the God who supplies is infinitely more reliable than a slot machine or a card table. The doctrine of providence is also central: God governs the details of life (Matt. 10:29-31), which means the person does not need to seize control through gambling. The future is in better hands than chance.
4.examples: A deacon's wife comes to the pastor in tears. She has discovered that her husband has secretly gambled away their retirement savings and taken out three loans against the house. He has been hiding it for four years. The pastor meets with the husband, who is devastated but also, for the first time, relieved to have been found out. The secrecy has been its own prison. The pastor's immediate steps: a doctor's referral (the man is clinically depressed), a financial counselor to map the debt, handing over all bank cards and internet access to his wife with his agreement, and the beginning of weekly biblical counseling. The deacon role is suspended -- not as punishment but as wisdom and accountability. The path is long and costly. But the man who sits in the pastor's office two years later, debts slowly being repaid, marriage rebuilt, is a man who has encountered grace at the bottom of the pit.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's definition of 'great gain' is the antithesis of the gambler's pursuit: not the jackpot but contentment. 'We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out' -- the gambler is playing a game with borrowed chips, on borrowed time, in a world they did not create and will not control. Contentment is the radical alternative: learning to receive what God provides as enough, because God himself is enough. This is not passivity -- it is the most counter-cultural posture possible in a world that constantly offers the next opportunity to get more.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content... I can do all things through him who strengthens me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Contentment is 'learned' -- it is not natural, not automatic, not the result of having enough. Paul learned it in prison, in shipwreck, in hunger. The gambler must learn it in financial ruin, in the wreckage of their choices. The strength to be content in poverty -- real poverty, the poverty that gambling often produces -- comes from Christ: 'through him who strengthens me.' This is not a self-help slogan; it is a theological claim. The person who has lost everything and still has Christ has not lost everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on... Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The anxiety that gambling medicates is named and addressed by Jesus directly. The gambler is often, at root, terrified -- about the future, about provision, about being enough. Jesus does not dismiss the anxiety; he redirects it toward the Father who feeds birds and clothes flowers. 'Are you not of more value than they?' The Father's care for the gambler is more certain than any winning hand. The counselor helps the person identify the specific anxiety driving the gambling and brings the Father's care to bear on it, specifically and repeatedly.

verseByVerse.quote: Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs is blunt about the economics of gambling: wealth sought by shortcuts shrinks. The wisdom of Scripture has always understood that sustainable provision comes through faithful work, honest dealing, and patient accumulation -- not through chance or scheme. The gambler's pursuit of the quick transformation of their circumstances is specifically what Proverbs warns against. The counselor uses Proverbs not to lecture but to reorient: 'This is God's wisdom about how provision actually works. Can we begin to trust his way instead of the other?'

5.title: When the Mind Breaks: Hearing Voices, Delusions, and Severe Mental Illness
5.overview:
Severe mental illness -- schizophrenia, psychosis, severe bipolar disorder with psychotic features -- is among the most challenging situations a pastor will face, and among the most important to handle correctly. The person who is hearing voices, holding fixed false beliefs (delusions), or has lost touch with reality is not primarily in need of biblical counseling. They are in need of a psychiatrist. The pastor's role here is not primary treatment but faithful presence alongside medical care.

See a doctor -- immediately: This is an emergency-level referral. A person in acute psychosis needs psychiatric assessment urgently. If they are a danger to themselves or others, emergency services must be called. Do not attempt to 'counsel' an acutely psychotic person -- engage gently, stay calm, and get medical help. Medication (antipsychotics) is typically essential and often life-changing. A person with schizophrenia who is stable on medication is a very different person from one who is not.

Biblically understood: Severe mental illness is a disorder of the brain -- a physical organ -- and is best understood as part of the suffering that the fall has brought upon the whole creation (Rom. 8:20-22). It is not demon possession (though demonic issues should not be dismissed entirely), it is not the result of specific personal sin, and it is not a failure of faith. The pastor who implies any of these to a suffering family does immense damage. The person with severe mental illness is a full image-bearer of God, loved by Christ, worthy of dignity and care.

The pastor's role: Be present. Visit. Pray. Sit with the family who is exhausted and bewildered. Ensure the church community does not abandon or stigmatise. Address whatever genuine spiritual needs can be addressed during stable periods -- with patience, simplicity, and great gentleness.
5.theology: The theology of suffering (Rom. 8:18-25; 2 Cor. 4:16-18) and the theology of the body (the brain is a physical organ subject to disease, as is the heart or the kidney) together provide the framework. Ed Welch's 'Blame It on the Brain?' is the essential resource here -- it carefully distinguishes between brain disease (which medicine addresses) and sin/heart issues (which biblical counseling addresses), while acknowledging that both can be present simultaneously. The person with schizophrenia may also have sin patterns that need to be addressed; the medication does not sanctify. But the bizarre beliefs and the heard voices are symptoms of a disordered brain, not a disordered will. Treating them as sin to be repented of is both theologically confused and pastorally cruel.
5.examples: A young man in the congregation begins behaving strangely -- staying up all night, speaking rapidly about grandiose plans, then becoming convinced that neighbours are spying on him. His parents, devout Christians, come to the pastor wondering if he needs deliverance. The pastor gently explains: 'What you are describing sounds like it may have a medical cause. Before anything else, I want you to take him to a doctor today -- a psychiatrist if possible.' The diagnosis is bipolar disorder with psychotic features. Medication stabilises him within weeks. The pastor visits him in hospital, reads the Psalms with him, and prays. The church rallies around the family. A year later the young man is stable, studying, and part of a small group. The pastor continues to meet with him monthly -- not to 'treat' him, but to disciple him in the ordinary means of grace, with patience and realistic expectations.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The fall corrupted the whole creation -- including the brain. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and psychosis are not spiritual failures or divine punishments; they are part of creation's groaning under the weight of the fall. The person with severe mental illness is suffering under a brokenness they did not choose, in a world that is not yet what it will be. The pastor who understands this will not heap spiritual blame but will weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15) and look forward to the day when 'the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption.'

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The person with severe mental illness, and the family around them, are often brokenhearted in the most literal sense. The pastoral gift is to bring this verse -- not as a cliche but as a reality: 'God is near to you right now, in this hospital room, in this bewildering season.' The Lord's nearness is not contingent on the person's mental stability or their ability to pray coherently. He is near to the brokenhearted as they actually are, not as they might be if they were well. This is the comfort the pastor carries into the ward.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's words were written in the context of physical suffering and persecution, but they speak powerfully into severe mental illness. The 'outer self' -- the brain, the body, the disordered mind -- is wasting or broken. But the inner self -- the person known and loved by God -- can still be renewed. And the suffering, however severe and however long, is producing something: 'an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison.' The counselor holds this eschatological hope for the person when they cannot hold it themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' pastoral policy toward the broken and barely-functioning. The person with severe mental illness is the bruised reed -- barely standing, fragile, close to breaking. The faintly burning wick -- dimly lit, more smoke than flame. Jesus does not break or quench them. He tends them with a faithfulness that no human carer can match. The pastor's role is to embody this tenderness -- to be present without demands, to pray without pressure, to love without conditions. The person may never be 'well' in the medical sense. They are still tended by the Servant who does not break bruised reeds.

6.title: Intrusive and Horrible Thoughts: OCD, Scrupulosity, and the Tormented Mind
6.overview:
Few people in a congregation suffer more quietly and more alone than those tormented by intrusive thoughts. These are unwanted, involuntary thoughts that horrify the person who has them -- thoughts of harming someone they love, blasphemous thoughts about God, sexual thoughts about inappropriate people, violent images that arrive without invitation. The person is not planning to act on these thoughts; they are desperately trying to make them stop. And the harder they try, the louder the thoughts become.

A particular Christian form is scrupulosity -- a form of OCD in which the person is tormented by doubt about their salvation, fear that they have committed the unforgivable sin, compulsive confession and re-confession, inability to accept forgiveness, and an exhausting cycle of religious ritual designed to neutralise the anxiety. These people are often the most sincere, most earnest Christians in the congregation -- and the most miserable.

See a doctor first: OCD has a strong neurological component. The brain's threat-detection system (the caudate nucleus) functions abnormally -- it sends 'danger' signals that do not switch off after reassurance, which is why reassurance-seeking makes OCD worse, not better. A doctor or psychiatrist should assess for OCD. Medication (SSRIs) can be significantly helpful. Specialised therapy (ERP -- Exposure and Response Prevention) is the evidence-based treatment. The pastor is not equipped to be the primary treatment provider.

Biblically understood: The critical pastoral error is to treat intrusive thoughts as intentional sin requiring repentance. The person tormented by blasphemous thoughts is not blaspheming -- they are horrified by the thoughts. The presence of a horrible thought is not the same as the choice to entertain it. James 1:14-15 describes the movement from temptation to sin: 'desire... gives birth to sin.' Intrusive thoughts are not desires; they are unwanted invasions. The pastor who demands repentance for thoughts the person did not choose and does not want crushes an already-crushed soul.
6.theology: Martin Luther himself suffered from what we would now recognise as severe scrupulosity -- tormented by fear that he had not confessed enough sins, that he was not truly forgiven, that God was his enemy. His confessor Staupitz directed him away from endless self-examination toward the finished work of Christ. This is the biblical counselor's task with the scrupulous person: not more examination but less -- a radical, repeated, patient redirection toward the cross. 'There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus' (Rom. 8:1) must be said again and again, not as a formula but as a reality. The assurance of salvation study is essential companion reading. The counselor must also resist the urge to provide reassurance -- reassurance is to OCD what food is to a hungry person: it satisfies briefly and increases the appetite.
6.examples: A young mother comes to her pastor in tears, convinced she is demonised. She has been having violent thoughts about her baby -- images of harm that appear in her mind unbidden and that terrify her. She has told no one for six months. The pastor's first response is critical: 'Thank you for telling me. The fact that these thoughts horrify you tells me something important: you do not want them. A person who actually wanted to harm their baby would not be sitting here weeping.' He explains the difference between involuntary thoughts and intentional sin. He refers her to her doctor that week. The diagnosis is postnatal OCD -- extremely common, treatable, and nothing to do with demonisation or spiritual failure. With treatment and pastoral support she recovers fully. The six months of silent torment need never have happened if someone had known what to look for.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: For the scrupulous person, this verse must be applied with surgical precision and repeated patience. 'No condemnation' -- not 'reduced condemnation,' not 'conditional condemnation,' not 'condemnation suspended pending your performance.' None. The counselor does not add conditions that Paul does not add: 'There is no condemnation -- provided you have confessed everything, provided you have not committed the unforgivable sin, provided your repentance was sincere enough.' Paul adds none of these. The counselor must not either. The scrupulous person's OCD will argue with the verse; the counselor's job is to keep bringing them back to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honourable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's instruction to direct the mind toward what is true and lovely is relevant -- but must be applied carefully with OCD sufferers, for whom 'don't think about it' paradoxically intensifies the intrusive thought. The counsel is not thought-suppression but thought-replacement: active engagement with Scripture, worship, service, and the things of God that crowd out the intruders. The goal is a mind so occupied with what is true and lovely that the intruders have less and less room. This is a slow process, not an instant fix.

verseByVerse.quote: But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This passage, rightly understood, is the pastoral key to intrusive thoughts. Sin begins with desire -- with the heart's willing movement toward what it wants. Intrusive thoughts are not desires; they are the opposite of desire. The person tormented by violent or blasphemous thoughts does not desire these thoughts -- they are appalled by them. The pastoral error is to collapse the distinction between 'a thought arrived' and 'I desired this thought.' The arrival of a temptation is not a sin; the willing, repeated, entertained nurturing of it is. The counselor who understands James 1 will not condemn the person for thoughts they did not choose.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Taking thoughts captive is the positive practice -- but again, must be applied with OCD wisdom. 'Captive' does not mean 'suppressed' or 'fought obsessively'; it means acknowledged, identified, and brought under the lordship of Christ. The practice is: notice the intrusive thought; name it ('that is an OCD thought, not a desire'); bring it to Christ ('Lord, I do not want this thought; I give it to you'); return to what is true (Phil. 4:8). This is not a magic formula but a practiced discipline that, over time, diminishes the power of the intrusions. The counselor models it and practices it with the person.

7.title: Trauma and Sexual Abuse: Walking Slowly with the Wounded
7.overview:
Trauma -- and sexual abuse in particular -- requires from the pastoral counselor a posture before it requires a technique: slowness, gentleness, absolute trustworthiness, and a willingness to listen without fixing. The person who has been sexually abused has had their bodily autonomy violated, their trust shattered (often by someone known to them), and their sense of the world as safe fundamentally destroyed. They may have been carrying this for years or decades in silence. The pastor who receives this disclosure is handling something extraordinarily precious and fragile.

See a doctor: A recent assault requires immediate medical attention (evidence preservation, physical injury, STI prevention). For historical trauma, the physical effects (chronic pain, sleep disorders, dissociation, hyper-vigilance) should be assessed medically. The pastor should also be aware that professional trauma-informed counseling is often necessary alongside pastoral care -- this is one of the areas where referral to a trained Christian counselor with trauma expertise is most important.

The first response to disclosure: Believe them. Do not ask questions that imply doubt. Do not minimise ('I am sure they did not mean it that way'). Do not rush to forgiveness ('you need to forgive them'). Do not immediately problem-solve. Simply receive what they have said with gravity and compassion: 'Thank you for trusting me with this. I am so sorry this happened to you. What happened to you was wrong.' These three sentences are worth more than an hour of theological explanation.

Legal and safeguarding responsibilities: If the abuse involved a minor or if there is ongoing risk, the pastor has legal and moral responsibilities to report. Never promise confidentiality before hearing a disclosure. Know your jurisdiction's mandatory reporting laws.

Addressing the heart over time: Shame inversion is the theological heart of trauma work -- the shame belongs to the perpetrator, not the victim. The person must be helped to understand that what was done to them was not their fault, is not who they are, and does not define their standing before God. Diane Langberg's work is essential here.
7.theology: The cross is the theological centre of pastoral trauma care. Jesus was violated -- betrayed, stripped, exposed, tortured, publicly shamed. He knows from the inside what violation feels like. 'For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin' (Heb. 4:15). The author of Hebrews does not say Jesus understands our weakness theoretically; he says he sympathises -- he has been there. The abused person who hears this -- who hears that Jesus was also exposed, also shamed, also violated by those with power over him -- finds a Saviour who is not above their suffering but inside it. And the resurrection means the story does not end in violation: restoration, dignity, and glory are the final word.
7.examples: A woman in her 40s discloses to her female pastor that she was sexually abused by her father throughout her childhood. She has never told anyone. She expects disbelief, dismissal, or a lecture on forgiveness. Instead the pastor says: 'I believe you. What he did to you was a terrible sin against you. You were a child. None of it was your fault.' The woman weeps for twenty minutes. Nothing is solved. No Scripture is quoted. No advice is given. The pastor simply stays. This session -- which felt to the pastor like she had 'done nothing' -- was later described by the woman as the moment her healing began. Being believed, in the presence of God, by a representative of God's community, after decades of carrying the secret alone -- this was profoundly healing. The theological word came later, in its own time.

verseByVerse.quote: For he has not despised or scorned the suffering of the afflicted one; he has not hidden his face from him but has listened to his cry for help. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God does not despise the suffering of the abused person. He does not turn his face away in disgust or embarrassment. He has not hidden his face -- he has listened. This is the word for the person who fears that God looks away from what was done to them, or that their suffering is too shameful for God to engage with. He has listened to the cry. The pastoral counselor who listens -- really listens, without flinching, without turning away -- embodies this verse. They are showing the person what God is like.

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The invitation to 'draw near with confidence' is directed at those who are weakest and most broken. The throne of grace is not for the strong and sorted; it is specifically for those who need mercy and grace in their time of need. The trauma survivor who has been taught that their abuse makes them unclean, unworthy, or unacceptable to God hears in this verse the direct contradiction of that lie. Come. Draw near. The High Priest who sympathises with weakness is waiting -- not with judgment but with mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives... to comfort all who mourn... to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus read this passage in the Nazareth synagogue and said 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:21). He identified his mission as binding up the brokenhearted and bringing liberty to captives. The trauma survivor is the brokenhearted; the shame and bondage of abuse is the captivity. This is not a distant hope but a present mission of Christ -- he is actively binding up and liberating. The counselor participates in Christ's own work when they sit with the wounded, listen, and point toward the One who turns ashes into beauty.

verseByVerse.quote: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. And he who was seated on the throne said, 'Behold, I am making all things new.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The eschatological promise is not escapism for the trauma survivor -- it is the guarantee that the story does not end with what was done to them. God will wipe away every tear -- including the tears they have wept alone in the night for decades. 'I am making all things new' -- the body that was violated, the trust that was shattered, the childhood that was stolen -- all of it is within the scope of God's renewal. The counselor holds this hope patiently, offering it not as a way to rush the person past their grief, but as the horizon toward which their slow, painful journey is headed.

8.title: Suicide and Self-Harm: Staying Close in the Darkest Place
8.overview:
Suicide is the pastoral emergency above all others. A person who is actively suicidal is in immediate danger of death, and the pastor's response in that moment may be the difference between life and death. This is not hyperbole -- it is the weight that pastoral care in this area carries, and the counselor must be prepared before the crisis arrives, not during it.

Emergency referral: If a person discloses active suicidal intent with a plan and means, do not leave them alone. Call emergency services or take them to an emergency room immediately. Your confidentiality obligation does not override the obligation to preserve life. Know your local crisis line numbers. Keep them in your phone.

See a doctor: For any disclosure of suicidal ideation or self-harm, a medical and psychiatric assessment is essential. Depression, bipolar disorder, and other conditions significantly elevate suicide risk and are treatable. Medication can save lives in this context. The pastor is not equipped to be the primary treatment provider and should not attempt to be.

Self-harm (cutting, burning, etc.) is often misunderstood. It is typically not a suicide attempt -- it is a way of managing overwhelming emotional pain that the person cannot otherwise process. It requires compassionate, non-shaming pastoral care and professional support, not moral condemnation.

Biblically understood: Suicidal ideation is almost always the product of profound suffering -- depression, despair, shame, trauma, loss -- rather than a straightforward sin issue. The person who wants to die is not primarily sinning; they are suffering beyond what they believe they can bear. The pastoral response is not a lecture on the sanctity of life (however true) but the presence of a person who will not leave, who will stay close, who will say: 'You matter. I am not going anywhere. Let us get you help right now.'

After the crisis: Long-term pastoral accompaniment is essential. Suicide loss bereavement (for those who have lost someone to suicide) also requires specific pastoral sensitivity -- grief, guilt, stigma, and unanswerable questions combine in a uniquely devastating way.
8.theology: The theology of lament is the pastoral framework for suicidal despair. The Psalms give language to a level of anguish that nothing else in Scripture matches: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Ps. 22:1); 'I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears' (Ps. 6:6); 'For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol' (Ps. 88:3). The person in suicidal despair is not beyond the Psalms -- they are in them. The counselor who can say 'the Bible knows this darkness; God is not shocked by your despair; even his servants have sat where you are sitting' gives the person something precious: permission to be honest with God, and the knowledge that honest darkness does not disqualify them from God's love. Elijah under the broom tree (1 Kings 19:4) -- 'It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life' -- is one of the most pastorally important passages in the Old Testament.
8.examples: A pastor receives a text message at 11pm: 'I don't think I can keep going.' He calls immediately. The person answers. He listens for twenty minutes without problem-solving. Then: 'I need to ask you directly -- are you thinking about ending your life?' The person says yes. 'Do you have a plan?' Yes. 'I am coming to you right now.' He drives to their house, stays with them through the night, and takes them to the emergency room in the morning. The person is admitted, medicated, and stabilised over two weeks. The pastor visits every other day. Two years later that person leads the church's mental health support group. The pastor's willingness to drive at midnight was not heroic -- it was simply what a shepherd does when a sheep is in the road.

verseByVerse.quote: But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.' And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, 'Arise and eat.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Elijah -- prophet of fire, man of extraordinary faith -- sits under a tree and asks to die. God's response is not rebuke but care: an angel touches him and says 'Arise and eat.' Before any word of theology, before any call to ministry, before any rebuke of self-pity -- food and rest. God meets the suicidal prophet at the level of his physical exhaustion. The pastoral lesson is profound: sometimes the first response to despair is not a sermon but a meal, not a theological correction but a warm presence and the practical care that says 'you matter enough for me to tend to your body.'

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, God of my salvation; I cry out day and night before you. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry! For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 88 is the darkest Psalm -- it ends with 'darkness is my closest friend' and offers no resolution. It is in the Bible. God put it there. This means the cry of absolute despair, the life that 'draws near to Sheol,' is not outside the scope of prayer or outside the bounds of faith. The person in suicidal despair who hears that Scripture itself speaks their language -- that God has not cleaned up this darkness but has given it a voice and preserved it for millennia -- finds something unexpected: company. They are not the first person to have sat in this darkness and addressed God from within it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life... nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise that nothing can separate us from God's love is the theological anchor for the suicidal person who fears that their despair has taken them beyond God's reach. 'Neither death nor life' -- not even the death they are contemplating, not even the life that feels unlivable. The love of God is not defeated by the depth of the darkness. The counselor returns to this verse again and again -- not as a formula, not as a pressure tactic ('God loves you so you must not do this'), but as the truth that outlasts the night: you cannot get to a place where God does not love you.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Not distant, not turning away, not overwhelmed by the depth of the brokenness -- near. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted. The person who feels most abandoned by God, most beyond the reach of hope, is precisely the person to whom God has drawn closest. The pastoral counselor embodies this nearness by staying -- by not flinching, by not retreating to theological safety, by remaining present in the darkness. The presence of the counselor is a sacrament of the nearness of God. 'I am here' -- said to the person in suicidal despair -- is one of the most theological things a pastor can say.

9.title: Domestic Violence and Abuse: Protecting the Vulnerable, Confronting the Powerful
9.overview:
Domestic violence and abuse is one of the most dangerous and most frequently mishandled situations in the church. It is dangerous because abusers are often charming, church-active, and skilled at presenting themselves as the victim. It is mishandled because pastors, trained in the theology of reconciliation, often apply marriage-preservation principles to a situation that requires safety-first principles -- and send an abused spouse back into danger with an admonition to be more submissive or to pray more.

Immediate safety first: Before any pastoral counsel, ask: 'Is this person safe right now? Are the children safe?' If there is immediate danger, the priority is safety -- a shelter, a safe house, emergency services if necessary. The pastoral conversation about the marriage comes later. Safety comes first, always.

See a doctor: Physical injuries need medical attention. Chronic stress from abuse also has significant medical effects. The doctor's record of injuries may also be legally important.

Biblically understood: Abuse is not a marriage problem to be fixed with better communication. It is a sin by the abuser against the victim -- a serious, persistent, often escalating pattern of domination, control, fear, and harm. Leslie Vernick distinguishes between a 'difficult marriage' and a 'destructive marriage' -- the latter requires a different response entirely. The biblical counselor's primary obligation in a destructive marriage is to the safety and dignity of the victim, not to the preservation of the marriage structure.

Confronting the abuser: The abuser must be confronted directly, firmly, and with accountability (Matt. 18:15-17). Church discipline is appropriate where the abuser is unrepentant. True repentance in an abuser is demonstrated over a long period -- not claimed in a tearful session immediately after exposure. The pastor who accepts a quick repentance and reconciles the couple rapidly is creating danger, not healing.

The victim and submission: The biblical teaching on wifely submission (Eph. 5:22-24) has sometimes been weaponised to keep victims in danger. This is a profound misuse of Scripture. Submission in Ephesians 5 is embedded in a passage about mutual submission (Eph. 5:21) and a husband's Christlike self-sacrifice (Eph. 5:25-29). A husband who uses submission teaching to justify abuse has neither understood nor obeyed the passage. A wife who leaves an abusive husband is not sinning against Scripture.
9.theology: The Ninth Commandment (you shall not bear false witness) and the Sixth (you shall not murder) together address abuse: the abuser bears false witness about the nature of the relationship, and the pattern of abuse -- physical, emotional, sexual -- is an assault on the image of God in the victim. Every person made in God's image has an inalienable dignity that no marriage vow, no cultural tradition, and no misapplied Scripture text can override. The church that protects abusers and silences victims has not understood either the justice of God or the care of God for the vulnerable. 'He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?' (Mic. 6:8). Justice for the vulnerable is not optional in God's community.
9.examples: A woman tells her pastor that her husband hits her when he is angry -- 'but only occasionally, and he always apologises.' The pastor's instinct is to offer marriage counseling. But first he asks: 'Are you safe at home? Are the children safe?' He learns that the violence has been escalating. He does not send her home with advice to be more patient. He says: 'What he is doing is wrong -- it is a sin against you and against God. Your safety and the children's safety is the priority right now. I want to help you make a plan to be safe.' He contacts a domestic violence resource and helps her make a safety plan. He then confronts the husband privately and clearly: 'What you are doing is abuse. It must stop completely and permanently. I want to help you, but there will be no reconciliation until there has been a sustained, verified change over a significant period of time.' The husband is initially defensive, then tearful, then -- over 18 months of accountability, counseling, and church oversight -- genuinely changed. The reconciliation, when it comes, is real. It nearly did not happen because the pastor nearly sent her home alone.

verseByVerse.quote: He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Justice -- mishpat -- is the first requirement named. Not peace, not reconciliation, not harmony -- justice. In the context of domestic abuse, justice means naming what is happening accurately (abuse, not 'conflict'), protecting the vulnerable from further harm, holding the powerful accountable, and refusing to sacrifice the victim's safety on the altar of the institution of marriage. The church that does justice in this area is walking humbly with its God. The church that protects its reputation at the expense of the victim is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The standard for a husband is not authority but sacrifice. 'As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her' -- Christ's love was cruciform, self-emptying, other-centred. The abusive husband who claims biblical authority while terrorising his family has inverted the passage entirely. He is claiming the authority without the sacrifice, the headship without the service, the submission of his wife without the Christlike love that alone makes submission possible and meaningful. The biblical counselor corrects this inversion directly and without apology: 'The Scripture you are using to justify your behaviour actually condemns it.'

verseByVerse.quote: Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalm addresses those in authority -- judges, rulers, leaders -- and commands them to rescue the weak from the hand of the wicked. The pastor in authority over a congregation is addressed here: rescue the weak. Not mediate between the weak and the wicked. Not balance the interests of both. Rescue. Deliver. This is not a small word. The pastor who understands this text will not offer 'both sides' pastoral neutrality in an abuse situation -- they will act, decisively and concretely, to protect the person being harmed.

verseByVerse.quote: If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone... But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you... If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Church discipline is the God-given structure for confronting serious, unrepentant sin -- and domestic abuse is serious, unrepentant sin. The process applies: private confrontation, escalation, church involvement, and, if necessary, formal discipline. The pastor who applies this faithfully is not being harsh -- he is following the Lord's own instructions for protecting the community from unrepentant sin and providing a structure within which the abuser might be reached by genuine accountability. The goal is always repentance and restoration -- but it is a restoration that takes a long time to verify, and that never comes at the cost of the victim's safety.
